abstract: Semaglutide and other GLP-1 receptor agonists are transforming obesity treatment, and patients often describe a quieting of intrusive food thoughts that motivate overconsumption of ultra-palatable foods, referred to as "food noise," yet it remains unclear which components of feeding behavior they act upon. Here, we designed a battery of behavioral tasks that separate the perceptual, hedonic, and motivational components of glucose intake in mice. Semaglutide impaired sweet taste categorization (in a psychophysical task) and induced conditioned taste avoidance not aversion, and thus left palatability intact. Its largest effect, however, was on motivation: it selectively disrupted the active pursuit of glucose and, to a lesser extent, lipids, sparing passive intake. In a novel lick-triggered taste alternation task, two fixed sippers delivered either glucose or a second tastant (e.g., saccharin or lipids), with the tastants swapping positions after a set number of licks. This design separated effortless consumption, when the swap brought glucose directly to the mouse (passive hit), from effortful pursuit requiring crossing to the opposite sipper (active hit). A single dose of semaglutide left passive hits intact, but markedly reduced active hits: mice readily exploited glucose that came to them, yet often failed to go after it. As the drug's effect waned, mice regained body weight by selectively overconsuming standard chow over glucose, and glucose over lipids, a shift in diet choice that persisted through the end of the experiment. Thus, semaglutide impairs the wanting, but not the liking, of glucose, providing (in mice) a behavioral correlate of the quieting of "food noise" reported by patients.
